column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 21: “Say: I believe in Allah — then be steadfast”

column2: From Sufyān ibn ʿAbdillāh (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, tell me something about Islam that I will not need to ask anyone but you about. He said: “Say: I believe in Allah — then be steadfast.” Muslim reported it.

Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from Sufyān. This Sufyān is Ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Thaqafī, of al-Ṭāʾif; he was a Companion, and was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's governor over al-Ṭāʾif.

It has also been narrated from Sufyān ibn ʿAbdillāh by other routes, with additions. Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded it through the narration of al-Zuhrī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Māʿiz (in al-Tirmidhī's version,

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Māʿiz), from Sufyān ibn ʿAbdillāh, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, tell me something to hold fast to. He said: “Say: My Lord is Allah — then be steadfast.” I said: Messenger of Allah, what do you fear most for me?
He took hold of his own tongue and said: “This.” Al-Tirmidhī said: ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded it through the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn Sufyān al-Thaqafī, from his father, that a man said: Messenger of Allah, command me with something in Islam that I will not need to ask anyone about after you. He said: “Say: I believe in Allah — then be steadfast.”
I said: Then what should I guard against?
He pointed to his tongue.

Sufyān ibn ʿAbdillāh's words to the Prophet ﷺ, “Tell me something about Islam that I will not need to ask anyone about after you,” were a request that he teach him a saying that would comprehend the whole matter of Islam and suffice him, so that he would need nothing else after it.
The Prophet ﷺ said to him: “Say: I believe in Allah — then be steadfast”; and in the other narration: “Say: My Lord is Allah — then be steadfast.”

This is drawn from the words of the Mighty and Majestic: “Indeed, those who said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast — the angels descend upon them, [saying,] ‘Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive glad tidings of the Paradise you were promised’” [Fuṣṣilat 41:30];

and from His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: “Indeed, those who said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast — no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve. Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding in it forever, as a reward for what they used to do” [al-Aḥqāf 46:13–14].
Al-Nasāʾī recorded in his Tafsīr, through the narration of Suhayl ibn Abī Ḥazm: Thābit told us, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ recited
“Indeed, those who said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast,” and said: “People have said it and then disbelieved; whoever dies upon it is among the people of steadfastness.”

Al-Tirmidhī recorded it in the wording: He said: “People have said it, then most of them disbelieved; whoever dies upon it is among those who remained steadfast.” He said: ḥasan gharīb. Suhayl has been criticised on account of his memory.
Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq said in explaining “then remained steadfast”: They did not associate anything with Allah.
It is also related from him: They did not turn to any god besides Him.
And from him: Then they remained steadfast in holding that Allah is their Lord.

From Ibn ʿAbbās, with a weak chain: This is the most lenient verse in the Book of Allah — “said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast” — steadfast upon the testimony that there is no god but Allah.
Something similar is narrated from Anas, Mujāhid, al-Aswad ibn Hilāl, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Suddī, ʿIkrimah and others.

It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb recited this verse on the minbar — “Indeed, those who said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast” — and said: They did not dodge about as a fox dodges.
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the words of the Exalted, “then remained steadfast”: They remained steadfast in fulfilling His obligations.
From Abū al-ʿĀliyah: Then they devoted their religion and their deeds sincerely to Him.
From Qatādah: They remained steadfast in obeying Allah. When al-Ḥasan recited this verse, he would say: O Allah, You are our Lord, so grant us steadfastness.

Perhaps those who said that the steadfastness meant is steadfastness upon tawḥīd meant only the complete tawḥīd that makes the Fire unlawful for the one who has it, which is the true realisation of the meaning of “There is no god but Allah.”
For a god (ilāh) is the one who is obeyed and never disobeyed, out of fear, reverence, awe, love, hope, reliance and supplication; and all sins impair this tawḥīd,

because they are a response to the one who calls to whim — that is, Satan. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Have you seen the one who takes his own whim as his god?” [al-Jāthiyah 45:23]. Al-Ḥasan and others said: He is the one who never desires anything without going after it. This is incompatible with steadfastness upon tawḥīd.
As for the narration of those who report “Say: I believe in Allah,” the meaning is clearer,

because faith (īmān) includes righteous deeds according to the Salaf and the hadith scholars who follow them. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “So be steadfast as you have been commanded, you and those who have repented with you, and do not transgress; indeed, He sees what you do” [Hūd 11:112].

He commanded him to be steadfast, he and those who repented with him, and not to go beyond what they were commanded, which is transgression; and He told them that He sees their deeds and is aware of them. The Exalted said: “So call [people] to that, and be steadfast as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires” [al-Shūrā 42:15].
Qatādah said: Muḥammad ﷺ was commanded to be steadfast upon the command of Allah.
Al-Thawrī said: Upon the Qurʾān. And from al-Ḥasan: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ girded himself in earnest, and was not seen laughing.
Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded it.

Al-Qushayrī and others mention that someone saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and said to him: Messenger of Allah, you said, “Hūd and its sisters have turned my hair grey.” What in it turned your hair grey?
He said: “His words: ‘So be steadfast as you have been commanded.’”
The Mighty and Majestic said: “Say: I am only a man like you; it is revealed to me that your god is one God, so be steadfast towards Him and seek His forgiveness” [Fuṣṣilat 41:6].

Allah the Exalted has commanded establishing the religion in general, as He said: “He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Nūḥ, and what We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Ibrāhīm, Mūsā and ʿĪsā: Establish the religion and do not be divided in it” [al-Shūrā 42:13];
and He commanded establishing the prayer in many places in His Book, just as He commanded steadfastness upon tawḥīd in those two verses.

Steadfastness (istiqāmah) is keeping to the straight path, which is the upright religion, without swerving from it to the right or the left. This includes doing all acts of obedience, outward and inward, and likewise leaving everything forbidden; and so this counsel comprehends all the qualities of the religion.
In His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, “so be steadfast towards Him and seek His forgiveness,” there is an indication that some shortfall in the steadfastness commanded is unavoidable,

and it is made good by seeking forgiveness, which entails repentance and returning to steadfastness. It is like the words of the Prophet ﷺ to Muʿādh: “Fear Allah wherever you are, and follow a bad deed with a good one that will wipe it out.”
The Prophet ﷺ told us that people will never be able to be steadfast as steadfastness truly requires, as Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Thawbān, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Be steadfast — and you will never manage it fully. Know that the best of your deeds is the prayer, and none guards his wuḍūʾ except a believer.” In a narration of Imam Aḥmad's: “Aim aright and come close, and none guards his wuḍūʾ except a believer.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Aim aright and come close.”
Aiming aright (sadād) is the reality of steadfastness: it is hitting the mark in all one's words, deeds and intentions, like someone who shoots at a target and hits it.

The Prophet ﷺ commanded ʿAlī to ask Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for right aim and guidance, and said to him: “By right aim, call to mind the aiming of your arrow; and by guidance, your being guided along the road.”
Coming close (muqārabah) is hitting near the target when one does not hit the target itself — but on condition that one is resolved on aiming aright and hitting the target,
so that coming close is not intentional. This is shown by the words of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of al-Ḥakam ibn Ḥazn al-Kulafī:

“O people, you will not do — or: you will not be able to do — all that I have commanded you; but aim aright and rejoice.” That is: intend to aim aright, to hit the mark and to be steadfast; for if they aimed aright in all their deeds, they would have done all that they were commanded.

The root of steadfastness is the heart's being steadfast upon tawḥīd, as Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq and others explained His words, “Indeed, those who said, ‘Our Lord is Allah,’ and then remained steadfast,” as meaning that they did not turn to anyone besides Him.
When the heart is steadfast in knowing Allah, fearing Him, revering Him, holding Him in awe, loving Him, seeking Him, hoping in Him, calling on Him,
relying on Him and turning away from all else, then all the limbs become steadfast in obeying Him. For the heart is the king of the limbs and they are its troops; when the king is upright,

his troops and subjects are upright. In the same way, His words, Exalted is He, “So set your face to the religion, inclining to the truth” [al-Rūm 30:30], have been explained as making one's intention sincerely for Allah and seeking Him alone, without partner.

After the heart, the limb whose steadfastness most needs watching is the tongue, for it is the heart's interpreter and gives expression to it. That is why, when the Prophet ﷺ had commanded steadfastness, he then counselled him to guard his tongue.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A servant's faith will not be upright until his heart is upright, and his heart will not be upright until his tongue is upright.”

In al-Tirmidhī's collection, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf (as the Prophet's words and as Abū Saʿīd's own): “When the son of Ādam wakes in the morning, all the limbs humble themselves before the tongue and say: Fear Allah concerning us, for we are only through you; if you are upright, we are upright, and if you are crooked, we are crooked.”
